1.title: Agentic Loops and stopreason
1.text: Welcome to Module one: Agentic Loops and stop reason. This module covers task statement one point one: design and implement agentic loops. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do four things. The agentic loop lifecycle: request, inspect stop reason, run the tools, return the results, repeat. How tool results are added to the conversation history. Model-driven decisions versus pre-configured decision trees or tool sequences. The anti-patterns that the exam names: parsing natural language, an iteration cap as the main stop, checking for assistant text.

1.title: Case Check-In: Birchwood Supply Answers a Return Request
1.text: Our running case is Birchwood Supply. Birchwood Supply Answers a Return Request. A customer writes: "My blender arrived cracked. I want my money back.". The support agent must look up the customer, find the order, check the return policy and issue a refund. Nobody knows in advance how many tool calls that takes: the agent decides step by step.

1.title: The Agentic Loop
1.text: The Agentic Loop. An agentic loop lets Claude work toward a goal over several steps. Each cycle has the same shape. Send a request to Claude with the conversation so far and the list of tools. Inspect stop reason in the response. If it is "tool use", Claude wants tools run: execute each requested tool in your code. Append the results to the conversation (the assistant message with the tool use blocks, then a user message with the matching tool result blocks) and send the next request. If it is "end turn", Claude has finished: stop the loop and present the final answer.

1.title: The Agentic Loop, continued
1.text: The Agentic Loop, continued. The figure shows this: The agentic loop: send the request, read stop reason, run the requested tools and append their results while stop reason is tool use, and finish when stop reason is end turn.

1.title: The Agentic Loop, continued
1.text: The Agentic Loop, continued. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study. Exam tip: The loop continues when stop reason is "tool use" and terminates when it is "end turn". Memorize both values and what each triggers.

1.title: How Tool Results Reach the Model
1.text: How Tool Results Reach the Model. The A P I (application programming interface) is stateless: Claude only knows what you send. After a tool runs, you must append the result to the history so the next request can reason about it. The history grows in pairs: the assistant message (text plus tool use blocks) and the user message carrying the tool result blocks, each linked by tool use id. Rules of the A P I: the tool result blocks must immediately follow the assistant's tool use message, and in that user message the tool result blocks must come first, before any text.

1.title: How Tool Results Reach the Model, continued
1.text: How Tool Results Reach the Model, continued. Claude may request several tools in one response (parallel tool use): run them all and return all the results in one user message. If a tool fails, return the error text in the tool result with is error: true so Claude can adapt instead of guessing.

1.title: How Tool Results Reach the Model, continued
1.text: How Tool Results Reach the Model, continued. The figure shows this: How the history grows: each tool use from the assistant is followed by a user message with the matching tool result, until the assistant ends the turn. Exam tip: The A P I is stateless: if a question says Claude "forgot" an earlier tool result, the history was not appended or resent.

1.title: Model-Driven Versus Pre-Configured
1.text: Model-Driven Versus Pre-Configured. Who chooses the next tool? Model-driven (agentic loop): Claude, from the context and the last tool results. Pre-configured (decision tree or fixed sequence): Your code, in a fixed order or rule set. Best for. Model-driven (agentic loop): Open-ended tasks where the path depends on what is found. Pre-configured (decision tree or fixed sequence): Predictable steps with a known order. Risk. Model-driven (agentic loop): The model may skip or reorder steps unless something enforces them. Pre-configured (decision tree or fixed sequence): Rigid; breaks on cases you did not foresee. Exam link. Model-driven (agentic loop): This task statement. Pre-configured (decision tree or fixed sequence): Used with the model-driven loop when order is mandatory (Module three).

1.title: Model-Driven Versus Pre-Configured, continued
1.text: Model-Driven Versus Pre-Configured, continued. The exam contrasts "Claude reasons about which tool to call next based on context" with "pre-configured decision trees or tool sequences". The agentic loop is the first. A fixed order that is required by the business is not solved by turning the whole agent into a decision tree; you add enforcement at the points that matter (Module three). Exam tip: "Claude decides the next tool from context" is the agentic (model-driven) pattern; "your code fixes the order" is pre-configured. A required order is enforced at specific points (Module three), not by dropping the loop.

1.title: Stopping the Loop Correctly
1.text: Stopping the Loop Correctly. The figure shows this: Stop on stop reason; do not stop on parsed text, on an arbitrary iteration cap, or on the mere presence of assistant text.

1.title: Stopping the Loop Correctly, continued
1.text: Stopping the Loop Correctly, continued. Parsing natural language ("if the reply says 'I'm done'"). Wording varies; a polite sentence can appear while a tool call is still pending. An arbitrary iteration cap as the main stop (for example five turns). Cuts off tasks that need more steps and wastes turns on easy ones; the cap hides the real signal. Checking for assistant text as a completion indicator. Claude often writes text together with a tool use block ("Let me look that up"). Use stop reason as the authoritative signal.

1.title: Stopping the Loop Correctly, continued
1.text: Stopping the Loop Correctly, continued. A maximum-turns or budget limit is still a good safety net against runaway loops; it is just not the primary stopping mechanism.

1.title: Other stop reasons
1.text: Other stop reasons. end turn. Meaning: Claude finished naturally. What to do: Present the answer. tool use. Meaning: Claude requests tool calls. What to do: Run them, append results, continue. max tokens. Meaning: The reply hit your max tokens limit. What to do: The output is cut off: raise the limit or continue the turn. stop sequence. Meaning: A stop sequence you set was produced. What to do: Handle as your design requires. pause turn. Meaning: A server-side tool loop paused. What to do: Send the response back to continue. refusal. Meaning: Claude declined the request. What to do: Handle as a refusal, do not retry blindly.

1.title: Other stop reasons, continued
1.text: Other stop reasons, continued. The Claude Agent S D K (software development kit) runs this loop for you: it keeps going until Claude replies with no tool calls, then returns a result whose subtype is success; limits such as max Turns end it with error max turns instead. As of eight November two thousand twenty-six.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Loop: Request to inspect stop reason to run tools to append tool result to repeat. Continue or stop: tool use equals continue, end turn equals stop. History: Append the assistant message (with tool use) and a user message with tool result blocks, matched by tool use id. Parallel calls: Several tool use blocks may come at once: run all, return all results together. Model-driven versus fixed: Claude chooses next tool from context (agentic) versus your code fixes the order (decision tree). Anti-patterns: Parse text for "done"; arbitrary iteration cap as main stop; treat any text as completion. Safety net: A max-turns or budget limit is fine as a guard rail, not as the main stop.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. Birchwood's support agent sometimes stops after Claude writes "Let me check that order for you" even though the same response contains a tool use block. The loop ends because it checks whether the response contains any text. What is the best fix? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. stop reason is the authoritative loop signal. Text can accompany a tool call, so text is not a completion indicator; a prompt tweak, a fixed count and a keyword search all keep a fragile signal.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. A developer ends the agent run after a fixed eight iterations because "most tasks finish by then". Several complex refund cases return incomplete answers. What is the root problem? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. A cap cuts off tasks that need more steps. Terminate on end turn; keep a cap only as a safety limit.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. After running a requested tool, what must the application do before the next request? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. The A P I is stateless; the model can reason about the result only if it is in the history it receives.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Which design uses model-driven decision making? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Model-driven means Claude chooses the next action from context. The other options are pre-configured sequences.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. Claude returns a response with stop reason: "tool use" containing three tool use blocks. What is the correct handling? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Claude may request several tools at once; run each and return all results together (each linked to its tool use id).

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. A team wants protection against runaway loops. Which statement is best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. A limit is a sensible guard rail, but the loop should normally end on end turn.

1.title: Practice Question 7
1.text: Question seven. A response arrives with stop reason: "max tokens" and the answer ends mid-sentence. What does this tell you? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. max tokens means the output limit was reached, so the answer is incomplete.

1.title: Practice Question 8
1.text: Question eight. Select two. Which two statements about the agentic loop are correct? The five options are on the screen. The answers are B and E. The loop runs on stop reason, and results travel back in a user message matched by tool use id. Keyword checks and fixed counts are fragile, and the A P I is stateless so the history must be resent.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all eight answers. Question one: A. Question two: D. Question three: D. Question four: D. Question five: A. Question six: D. Question seven: A. Question eight: B and E. In the next module, we continue the course.
